observations: Accepted by operator decision on 2026-09-24. The campaign's question was whether the FerroForge conversion changed flight behaviour, not whether the aircraft is tuned; the operator judged that question answered and the firmware safe. The deviations from the procedure as written are recorded below rather than scoped away, and the procedure is unchanged for future candidates.

The control law is measurably identical across the conversion. P recovered from closed-loop data as pid/error is 0.25/0.25/0.20 on both sides, matching the configured 2.5/2.5/2.0 with the stored-units factor of ten, over roughly 133000 armed samples spanning pre-conversion flights 1-2 and post-conversion flights 15, 19, 21 and 22.

Loop timing is identical across the conversion: about 84000 intervals, every one alternating 2000/3000 us at 50/50, which is a 400 Hz loop sampled by a 1 kHz monotonic. Not one deviation in either era.
Zero sequence gaps, zero repeated samples and zero CRC failures across roughly 10 MB of recovered logs.
Flight 16 is the clean hover hop: 4.0 s airborne, motors 331..904 with worst spread 165 and no saturation, ending at 7 deg/s before a quiet disarm.

The arm boundary is clean on flight 16: peak |pid| of 6 over the first 0.25 s airborne with commands at zero, so no retained integral or command history crosses the arm boundary. This is bounded evidence for one boundary, not proof of every internal reset path, and I stays zero.

The loop survived violence without missing a cycle. Flight 22 reached 1592 deg/s with the mixer saturated on 28 commands and yaw PID pinned at -2000, and the control sequence has no gap through any of it: no watchdog reset, no dropped cycle, no logging fault.

Zero-throttle behaviour is correct: in flight 21 the PID demanded correction at 997 deg/s while all four motors sat at zero, so the aircraft tumbled freely rather than the controller fighting with no authority.

The operator attributes every ground contact to deliberately putting the aircraft down in a confined field rather than flying it into a boundary, and reports no loss of control caused by the control system.

Oscillation review resolved with tools/blackbox_analyzer.py. No axis is classified as high-frequency or noise-like in any flight of either era, and peak content sits at 0.8-3.5 Hz throughout - airframe motion, not oscillation. Nothing appears in the 10-13 Hz band that withdrew roll P 3.0.

The analyzer's own metrics match across the conversion: control interval 2500.0 us with std 500 us and zero intervals over 3000 us, IMU rate 1011.8 Hz pre against 1012.3 Hz post, zero missing BB2 frames, and 0.0 ms filter lag - pre-conversion flight 2 against post-conversion 16, 21 and 22.
limitations: Command tracking was not evaluated. Every flight with stick input (19, 21, 22) ended in deliberate ground contact, and every flight that ended cleanly (12, 15, 16, 20) was flown with centred sticks - commanded rate 0.0 on roll and pitch. No single flight combined separated inputs with a controlled landing, so the procedure's step 3 was not satisfied and no commanded-versus-measured comparison is claimed.

Stop conditions listed by the procedure were observed in flights 19, 21 and 22: rapid attitude departure, mixer saturation in flight 22, and gyro clipping at the sensor's 2000 deg/s limit in flight 19. They are recorded as observed and attributed by the operator to intentional ground contact, not to control behaviour.
Analysis used both a dependency-free decoder written for this session and the project analyzer, tools/blackbox_analyzer.py, which reads .fwbb directly.
Battery current remains uncalibrated, carried forward from BENCH-FOX-001.
